item.title: Nasa's Swift burns up, highlighting challenges of boosting satellites
item.description: Failed attempt to rescue Nasa's Swift observatory highlights the technical and fuel challenges facing the emerging satellite servicing industry ...
item.dc:creator: Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba
item.content:encoded: Nasa’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on October 20, 2026, while orbiting about 275 kilometres above Earth. Nasa ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady. The telescope reentered the atmosphere on November 4 above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent observing powerful cosmic explosions. Swift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026. LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, reentered Earth's atmosphere in September. The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first. As a PhD candidate in aerospace engineering, I know that rescuing satellites is hard. I research how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably. Swift’s loss points to a new hazard for the young industry that repairs, refuels and moves spacecraft around in orbit. If something goes wrong, the spacecraft doing the rescuing can become another problem. The rescuer started spinning The plan was for LINK to approach Swift, grab it with one of its three robotic arms and fire its thrusters to push the telescope back up to about 600 kilometres above Earth's surface, where it could keep observing for years. In late July, LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels, which are heavy wheels inside a spacecraft that help it turn without using fuel. That loss, combined with problems with its propulsion system, sent the spacecraft into an uncontrolled spin. Without working wheels, a spacecraft steers with its thrusters instead, and every burn spends propellant. Engineers eventually slowed LINK’s rotation by firing its thrusters against the spin. Nasa reported in August that they had cut its spin from about nine degrees per second to roughly one and a half degrees per second. Nasa and Katalyst Space, LINK’s builder, called off the capture and boost later in August. The team still flew LINK within 12 to 15 kilometres of Swift, where it deployed LINK’s three robotic arms and tested its electric thrusters. It never got close enough to grab the telescope. Fuel is the rescue budget A servicing spacecraft, like LINK, launches with a finite supply of propellant. Engineers split that fuel supply among the mission's jobs, from reaching the target and approaching it safely to capturing it and moving it to a new orbit. They also pack some extra fuel in case of surprises. Think of a tow truck that burns most of its gas getting itself out of a ditch. Even if it reaches a broken-down car, it may not have enough fuel left to tow it home. That scenario is close to what happened to LINK. Even after engineers brought its spin under control, Katalyst said the spacecraft no longer had enough propellant to capture Swift and raise its orbit safely. A fuel budget that covers only the planned steps leaves nothing for recovering from a fault. But every extra pound of propellant also makes a spacecraft heavier, and heavier spacecraft cost more to launch and take more fuel to move. Speed buys time and costs backup Starting in 2024, solar activity swelled Earth’s upper atmosphere, and the extra drag pulled Swift down faster than expected. Once Nasa saw how quickly Swift was falling, the agency had to move fast to try to save the observatory. Space missions typically take years to develop and launch, but in this case, a slow, conventional development programme risked arriving too late.  Nasa awarded Katalyst a $30 million contract in September 2025. The company had less than a year to design, build, test and launch LINK. LINK launched on July 3, 2026. Speed comes with trade-offs. In engineering, a compressed schedule can leave less time for repeated testing, building spare hardware and planning recovery options. Public reports do not say whether that trade-off played any part in LINK’s faults. Nasa has said that even though LINK didn’t succeed, the effort gave the agency experience in quickly building, launching and operating a servicing spacecraft. Engineers also showed they could upload new control software to steady a damaged servicing spacecraft with the hardware it had left. And LINK tested its arms and fired all three thrusters at once in orbit. What comes next While Swift was the most pressing case for a boost mission, it’s not the only one. Nasa’s Hubble Space Telescope could one day use a similar boost, and news reports suggested it would have been next in line had this mission worked. Future missions are pursuing two complementary approaches for rescuing satellites. Astroscale's ELSA-M is built to capture satellites that carry a docking plate installed before launch, which would make it easier for a rescuer to snag and boost them if the satellite eventually got into trouble. The European Space Agency’s ClearSpace-1 is planned for 2029 and aims to capture the Proba-1 satellite, which doesn't have a docking plate or anything to help ClearSpace-1 capture it, and remove it from orbit.LINK’s mission showed that a rescue takes more than a robotic arm and enough thrust to reach a target. It also takes a servicer spacecraft that can stay stable, recover from its own faults and keep enough propellant reserved to finish the job. In Swift’s case, the rescuer fell short before the rescue could begin.  (The writer is from University of Florida)

item.title: Enterprises face a reckoning in their AI costs as budgets come under strain
item.description: As AI adoption accelerates, companies are turning to model orchestration, smaller language models and token monitoring to control rising costs and improve returns on AI investments.
item.dc:creator: Avik Das
item.content:encoded: In April, Uber exhausted its entire 2026 budget for artificial intelligence (AI) after pushing engineers to adopt the technology faster. Adoption of Anthropic’s Claude Code — first rolled out in December — jumped to 84 per cent in March, up from 32 per cent just a month earlier. What the company seemingly failed to anticipate was a growing disconnect between the push for higher token usage and the teams controlling the spending, triggering an emergency slowdown.

item.title: Coca-Cola's India bottling arm HCCH files DRHP for 997.5 million-share IPO
item.description: The proposed IPO will be entirely an offer for sale by promoter Hindustan Coca-Cola Overseas Holdings, with no proceeds going to HCCH; the company reported ₹11,663 crore in FY26 revenue ...
item.dc:creator: Sharleen Dsouza
item.content:encoded: Hindustan Coca-Cola Holdings Limited (HCCH), the holding company of Coca-Cola's Indian bottling business, has established a dominant position in the Southern and Western parts of the country through a multi-year re-franchising process. “Our business and operations have undergone changes as a result of a multi-year re-franchising process. Between financial years 2024 and 2026, we sold our business undertakings in Rajasthan, Bihar, Jharkhand, Northeast India, parts of West Bengal and North Gujarat (collectively, the “Refranchised Units”) to other TCCC Bottlers by way of slump sales,” the firm said in its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) filed on Saturday.  It has the licence to prepare, package, distribute, and sell The Coca-Cola Company’s (TCCC) beverages exclusively in 10 states and four union territories, keeping its operations concentrated in the South and West.  HCCH can sell in all of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and the Union Territories of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and Lakshadweep. It faces restrictions in Diu, parts of Puducherry and Karaikal and Mahe.  In areas where it operates, the bottler had a network of 2,273 distributors as of June 30, 2026 and over half of them have been with the company for over five years.  Its production footprint comprises 14 owned production facilities with an aggregate installed capacity of 1,291.1 million unit cases per annum, supported by eight co-pack units. “Collectively, these facilities operated 90 bottling lines, including 77 owned bottling lines and 13 bottling lines at co-pack units, and were complemented by a network of 23 warehouses,” it said.  India was one of the five largest markets for the Coca-Cola System by unit case volume for calendar year 2025, the DRHP stated.  “Our recent strategic reorientation encompassing completion of the re-franchising process, addition of Jubilant Beverages as one of our promoters, leadership and organisational enhancements, and renewed focus on execution, has, we believe, established our foundation for future growth,” HCCH said.  The proposed initial public offering (IPO) comprises an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 997.5 million equity shares with a face value of ₹10 by promoter Hindustan Coca-Cola Overseas Holdings Pte. Ltd. The entire proceeds from the offer will go to the promoter selling shares. Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages, the primary bottling unit of HCCH, is one of Coca-Cola's largest bottling partners in India. Coca-Cola's decision to dilute its stake in its Indian bottling business is part of a larger global strategy to move away from bottling operations and adopt an asset-light, franchise-led business model. Its portfolio of brands includes Coca-Cola, Thums Up, Sprite, Fanta, Limca, Monster, Schweppes, Kinley, Maaza and Minute Maid. Currently, Hindustan Coca-Cola Overseas Holdings Pte. Ltd. holds 60 per cent of HCCH's equity share capital, while Jubilant Beverages Limited holds the remaining 40 per cent. Jubilant Beverages became one of the promoters of HCCH in July 2025. The book-running lead managers for the IPO are Kotak Investment Banking, Citi Global Markets India, J.P. Morgan India, Morgan Stanley India, Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs India and IIFL Capital Services. HCCH's profit attributable to shareholders stood at ₹408.45 crore in the April-June quarter, compared to ₹1,054.4 crore in the year ago period. Its revenue from operations rose 17 per cent to ₹4,310.17 crore during the period. In FY26, its revenue from operations stood at ₹11,663.24 crore, compared to ₹12,869.54 crore in FY25, down 9 per cent. The company was the largest non-alcoholic ready-to-drink beverage company by revenue operating exclusively in India in FY26, the DRHP said citing a report by The Knowledge Company (TKC). It stated that it has the highest market share of 37.2 per cent in the overall soft drinks and packaged drinking water category. In the still category, which includes its brands Maaza and Minute Maid, it has a market share of 42.6 per cent. It has a market share of 12.9 per cent in the energy drinks segment and 9.7 per cent in the packaged drinking water segment.
